speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Welcome to the Q1 2024 conference call. You can find the slides of this call on the sanofi.com Investors Page. I'd like to remind you that the information presented in this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to substantial risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially. I encourage you to read the disclaimer in our presentation. In addition, I refer you to our Form 20-F on file with the SEC for a description of these risk factors. I'm pleased to welcome our new CFO, François, to the presentation, who will be followed by Houman, our Head of R&D on the pipeline. For Q&A, we have Brian, Olivier, Thomas, and Julie to cover the global business units and Roy, our GC. For the Q&A, you have two options to participate. In Zoom, you can raise your hand to submit your questions in Q&A, which have been explained on the slide. Let's turn to the business. We had an excellent start in 2024 with 7% sales growth, in line with our fast-moving portfolio transformation. Growth was driven by launches, including new and existing indications for Dupixent, and this performance fully underpins our 2024 EPS guidance as CEO. Dupixent continues to increase penetration in all approved indications, and we saw performance diversified further across all geographies, plus, of course, the usual US insurance plans. Pharma launches were led by Nexviazyme and Altuviiio, with more details to come a little later. Launches also boosted the performance in Vaccines with Beyfortus making further progress, including in countries in the southern hemisphere. In Consumer Health, growth of 9% reflected the consolidation of the Qunol acquisition as well, of course, as organic growth. We're progressing the plan to separate this business as discussed in the past. Overall, we're pleased with the ongoing portfolio transformation, which is becoming more visible, also in our cost lines, with more resources going into the pipeline and less into SG&A. This is exactly the development we set out last year when we announced the next chapter of our strategy. Before moving on, I'd like to extend my thanks to all the Sanofi colleagues for their dedicated work and their commitment to patients and science to improve people's lives. Dupixent continues to perform strong demand-driven growth, with sales of more than €2.8 billion in the first quarter. Sales of this unique medicine increased by 25% globally, fueled by accelerated growth from indication expansions in the ex-U.S. markets, where sales grew as much as 51%. With now more than 850,000 patients worldwide, the strong contribution from countries like Japan, China, and Germany highlights the tremendous growth potential for Dupixent across all indications and geographies. In the U.S., sales exceeded €2 billion in the quarter, up 17%. U.S. growth reflects the customary dynamics of the annual reset of insurance plans. Almost eight years into its initial U.S. launch in atopic dermatitis, this effect underscores the large size and rapid growth of Dupixent, with leadership positions in new prescriptions across all five approved indications. As we look ahead to Q2, we remain very excited about the outlook for Dupixent's outstanding commercial success across all geographies, supported by regulatory progress towards launching multiple new indications in major markets. With our strong Q1 performance, we're extremely confident in delivering our previously communicated objective of around €13 billion in sales for the full year. As one of the leading medicines in immunology, respiratory is a core disease area for Dupixent, well ahead of any other competing biological medicine. Dupixent has established and maintained a distinct leadership position in new prescriptions among pulmonologists across asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps in the U.S. We believe in the growing importance of pulmonologists in adopting biologics to treat respiratory diseases, but we are also confident that their growing familiarity with Dupixent in type 2 inflammation will play a key role in the adoption of Dupixent as the potentially first advanced therapy in COPD in more than a decade if approved. We also continue to build a growing body of scientific evidence around Dupixent in addressing airway inflammation in the VESTIGE study, which was recently presented at the Quadruple AI Congress. Dupixent demonstrated reduced airway inflammation of mucus plugging in functional respiratory imaging in-house. We have an ambition to potentially introduce a new standard-of-care with Dupixent in COPD for patients with type 2 inflammation. As you may recall, significant regulatory progress has been achieved with Dupixent's potential in COPD across key markets. We are preparing for a potential launch in the U.S. as early as late June if approved by the FDA and plan for additional potential approvals in Europe and China by the end of the year. We're excited about the outlook for Dupixent's potential to become a breakthrough medicine for COPD, a leading cause of death worldwide. Dupixent is well-positioned to potentially address the high unmet need in COPD with a strong clinical profile across two large Phase 3 studies and more than seven years of real-world data on safety across five approved indications. Dupixent addresses the unmet medical need of a well-defined population of roughly 300,000 patients in the U.S. alone, whose disease is driven by type 2 inflammation and is uncontrolled despite standard-of-care therapies. COPD is a historically difficult disease area and a heterogeneous disease, with multiple development failures in the last decade. Over time, many patients become resigned to their medical condition with an experienced team that has a track record of development and commercial excellence in respiratory. We planned a targeted approach to drive the awareness and identification of COPD with type 2 inflammation among patients and pulmonologists. As we've seen with our launches across other major indications, the adoption of Dupixent as the first and only biologic in the COPD indication will require some time initially, and the inflection of sales growth is most likely to come in 2025 after the U.S. launch. We are confident that if approved, COPD will become the next major growth pillar for Dupixent. Together with our second potential blockbuster developed for COPD, itepekimab, we continue to expect peak sales of more than €5 billion for both products combined. Let's now move to the new launches, as Q1 further demonstrates our ability to execute successful launches and bring new medicines to patients. This quarter, all our new launches, including Beyfortus, made up close to €1 billion in sales or 9% of our total biopharma business. Beyfortus continued its global rollout in the quarter with the launch in the Southern Hemisphere countries of all interim protection programs in some Australian states and Chile. As RSV is seasonal, Beyfortus will have a sales pattern similar to that of flu vaccines. Nexviazyme grew strongly from new patients as well as patients converting from older medicines in the Pompe franchise. We're pleased with the overall growth in franchise sustainability. ALTUVIIIO is soon annualizing its launch. It has seen continued strong uptake, with most of the growth coming from other factor medicines and even some uptake from patients not on factor medicines. This shows us how innovation can help to revitalize hemophilia and grow Sanofi's total share. Other launched medicines also did well, including Sarclisa approved in multiple myeloma. Taking a closer look at Beyfortus, we’re really focused on the impact of improving public health and benefit for thousands of families. We've now real-world results from last year's implementation of broad immunization programs in the U.S., France, and Spain with Beyfortus. The results are strikingly impressive, showing a dramatic reduction in hospitalizations. The U.S. CDC recently published our effectiveness data for Beyfortus at 90%, and in Europe, we've seen similar results for hospitalization reduction across France and Spain. Overall, following the first season in the three launch countries where Beyfortus is used for all-in-from protection, this means that nearly 40,000 hospitalizations have already been avoided for families. This is the impact that matters most. This also provides perspective for Beyfortus’ global health benefit as we plan to launch in additional countries in H2. Together with AZ, we're working with regulatory authorities and extending the manufacturing network to make Beyfortus more available for the upcoming season, as we're glad to see such enthusiastic demand. We're confident that we will meet anticipated customer demand and look forward to extending all-in-from protection programs in the upcoming Northern Hemisphere RSV season. On my final slide, I wanted to highlight some progress on our ESG ambition exemplified by the work of our Global Health unit. Since its launch in 2021, the essential medicines from our GHC portfolio have supported close to 550,000 patients suffering from noncommunicable diseases in 31 countries, aiming to reach two million NCD patients by 2030. An additional differentiator is the meaningful work done by our teams to help build sustainable healthcare systems through partnerships with Ministries of Health, training of healthcare professionals, and our impact investment fund focused on supporting exclusive start-ups and businesses. I now have great pleasure in handing over to François, our new CFO.

speaker: François-Xavier Roger
title: CFO
content: Thank you, Paul. I'm pleased to have joined the team here at Sanofi earlier in April, and I'm looking forward to interacting with all of you in the future. Sales were up 7% in the quarter, and as Paul mentioned, growth was driven by our ongoing portfolio transformation towards biopharma medicines, with Dupixent sales up by 25% and the new launches, including Beyfortus, up by 150%. Excluding the impact of AUBAGIO's loss of exclusivity and COVID-19, growth was 12%. This analysis does not aim at removing all headwinds, but simply illustrates what the new Sanofi may look like in the future. The gross margin at 73.5% was down by 2.6 percentage points, mainly due to AUBAGIO and due to the absence of COVID-19 vaccine sales this year. In addition, the quarter was impacted by a one-off inventory adjustment to reflect declining standard costs. R&D expenses increased by 12% at constant exchange rates in line with our ambition to invest more in our pipeline. Resources are being deployed to advance late-stage immunology and neurology projects. SG&A increased by less than 3%, below half of sales growth, illustrating our strategic reallocation of resources. Our business operating margin decreased to 27.2%, mainly due to the gross margin decline, the step-up in R&D expenses, and an increase in profit sharing with Regeneron. As expected, EPS was down 7.4% in Q1, also partly impacted by a higher tax rate. Just one word on cash flow. It will be impacted in 2024 by our lower business operating income and by the phasing of rebate payments in the U.S. related to prior year sales. Let me now give you some additional information on our coming quarter. In Q2 2024, we expect Dupixent and the new pharma launches to grow further, while we continue to see the impact of the Aubagio loss of exclusivity in Europe. Notably, we don't expect any Beyfortus sales in Q2 due to early delivery in Q1 in some Southern Hemisphere countries, while shipments in Northern Hemisphere countries are not expected before the second half of 2024. For the full year 2024 sales outlook, we expect Dupixent to reach around €13 billion and the vaccine franchise to grow mid-single-digit, with Beyfortus anticipated to reach blockbuster status. The Aubagio loss of exclusivity will continue to impact the top line, mainly in H1. Finally, planned divestments will lower our sales by around €300 million over the year. For the full year P&L, we expect our gross margin to decrease slightly due to Aubagio and the absence of COVID-19 sales revenues this year. OpEx is expected to grow with about €700 million step-up in R&D, while SG&A expenses are expected to remain stable. Finally, our tax rate will increase to around 21% due to the implementation of the OECD Pillar 2. We confirm our full year 2024 expectation of a low single-digit decline in our business EPS at constant exchange rates. Excluding the impact of the higher tax rate, the full year 2024 business EPS is expected to be roughly stable. On foreign exchange, we foresee a negative currency impact to EPS of around 6% based on April 2024 average exchange rates. As a reminder, we continue to anticipate strong business EPS rebounds in 2025. As we have mentioned earlier, in 2024, we are transforming the company for long-term value creation. With that, I will now hand over to Houman.

speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: Thank you, François. We've seen substantial positive pipeline progress already in Q1, where we continue to deliver a consistent news flow of clinically important data and scientific publications and congresses. Frexalimab's encouraging Phase 2 data and multiple choices was recently published in the New England Journal, updated with data from the 48-week open-label extension, which we presented last week at the AAN Conference supporting our commitment to MS patients. In atopic dermatitis, we have the potential to further establish our leadership with amlitelimab, where we presented the Phase 2b data at AAD, showing largely sustained effects of amlitelimab on atopic dermatitis symptoms after 52 weeks of dosing. On the regulatory side, we've reached an impressive pace of approvals with two for Dupixent in multiple indications across different countries. FDA discussions regarding Dupixent's sBLA in COPD are ongoing under the priority review process, as Paul has mentioned. Amlitelimab, our non-depleting OX40 ligand monoclonal antibody, has shown potential best-in-class efficacy with a durable clinical response rate after 52 weeks from the STREAM AD Phase 2b study. The responder percentage is reflected in the IIGA 0/1 and the EG75 scores, which are both surrogate endpoints for AD, maintained and still significantly effective, even following withdrawal from the drug at week 24. The enrollment of all 4 Phase III studies is on track for the first regulatory submission expected in 2027. Frexelimab, our CD40 ligand antibody, shows high-efficacy non-lymphocyte depleting potential for MS with multiple indications under development. Most importantly, in relapsing remitting MS, the 48-week data from the Phase II open-label extension study demonstrated a sustained reduction of disease activity monitored by a mean number of gadolinium-positive type 1 lesions appearing on MRI. It is worthy to mention that nearly every patient on frexelimab IV exhibited no new lesions at a near-zero annualized relapse rate at 48 weeks. So, as you can see from the bar chart, patients switched from the placebo arm to the frexelimab arm, both IV and subcutaneous, showed impressive decreases in MS. The Phase III studies for relapsed remitting MS and NRPMS have initiated, with the first regulatory submission expected in 2027. We want to focus on rilzabrutinib, our oral BTK inhibitor, one of our 12 priority medicines. We've received a positive readout from the LUNA 3 Phase III study in ITP, a rare autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by abnormally low levels of platelets, persistent disabling fatigue, and increased hemorrhage. These results confirmed the positive Phase II data, with additional details to be presented at forthcoming medical meetings and a regulatory submission later this year. Alongside this positive news, we've received more Phase II data in asthma, confirming previous positive trends. We are very excited to present this data at the ATS conference next month. In February, we shared positive data for the third indication, CSU, at the AAI AI Annual Meeting, with Phase III starting later this year. These datasets are important stepping stones in our R&D transformation journey, emphasizing our commitment to rare diseases and the significant potential of BTK inhibitors. Additionally, we recently reshaped our overall oncology strategy, focusing on areas where we can make a meaningful difference based on our expertise in immunology. Our goal is to target critical unmet medical needs for patients benefiting from immune mechanisms. I want to finish by highlighting the upcoming Phase III and Phase II readouts and regulatory submissions expected in 2024 and 2025. As you can see, news flow will increase and become busier as we move into 2025, supported by the step-up in R&D investments that François just mentioned. I'm enthusiastic and eager as the news flow becomes richer and better, thanks to the growing pipeline and clinical study efforts. With this, I will hand back to Paul.

speaker: Brian Foard
title: SVP, U.S. Commercial Operations
content: Yeah. Thank you so much for the question. Really, as we get ready for the launch in COPD, first and foremost, it all starts with the patients. And I think what we've seen with this brand is that by going into diseases driven by underlying type 2 inflammation, we've really opened up new treatment opportunities for these patients and transformed a lot of patients' lives. As Paul mentioned, there are over 850,000 patients already on therapy. Many of those happen to be asthma sufferers and are treated by the pulmonologist community. So as you can imagine, as we've spoken with pulmonologists, they're extremely excited about having potentially a new option to treat these patients, who are currently on the highest dose of therapy and still exacerbating. So we must contextualize this properly. And you saw our reductions in both the BOREAS and areata trials, showing how effective they were at adding reduction in exacerbation rates of 30% and 34%. So we're very positive about this. The challenge with this particular patient population is probably less about the patients themselves and more about the fact that when you bring a new therapy like this after more than 10 years, it will take a little bit of time for the biologic ramp. Even though there's a burden of disease there for the patients, it will take some time for physicians to use biologics. That said, the pulmonologist community does use biologics today. So we feel like we're well-prepared and are creating a good marketplace for it.

speaker: Paul Hudson

title: Head of R&D
content: Yeah. Hi, Peter. You asked a very specific question about the patient burden of disease and patient population. We were very specific about our stratification strategy; we thought very deeply about the EOs concentration in the blood and specifically the phenotype. We focused specifically on what we saw in the Phase II data, and that reflected an outstanding reduction in the exacerbations in our Phase III studies. I think it's really important to recognize that as Sanofi goes forward, our development strategy is laser-focused to enable launch in the highest unmet medical need population. And that's what we've done. So that's why we have confidence in the way this population launch will expand.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO

speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: Let me begin by saying that Brian and I will collaborate on this response. Luisa, thank you for your question. You’ve raised two important topics: ITP and asthma tolerability. I'll address them directly. There continues to be a significant unmet medical need in ITP, as 50% of patients do not receive adequate care, especially regarding the stability of their platelet count. Many also experience considerable fatigue. I take great pleasure in developing Rilzabrutinib, especially as I've cared for these patients. This treatment is compelling for several reasons. It inhibits the production of B cells as a result of BTK inhibition and also prevents the phagocytosis of platelets, which helps to lower their count. This mechanism is particularly interesting when compared to the current standard of care, which inadequately addresses the needs of half of the patients and can necessitate extreme dietary changes. This creates a significant opportunity. Regarding tolerability, so far, the results have been quite encouraging in every aspect, which is exciting. As for your question about asthma, we shared our latest asthma data last year, and we remain enthusiastic about it. The potential for Rilzabrutinib to be the first oral treatment for advanced asthma is extraordinary, as it could transform the treatment approach compared to existing therapies. I am genuinely excited to invite everyone on this call to attend the ATS meeting to see the outcomes of our study, which we are eager to present. Now, to provide a broader perspective on the market, I’ll turn it over to Brian.

speaker: Brian Foard
title: SVP, U.S. Commercial Operations
content: I think it's a really good question. As you saw on R&D Day, when we started to talk about the 12 assets, this was one of those that we discussed. This treatment can be really differentiated versus the competition in each of those therapeutic areas. Now specifically about ITP and to provide a broader context, we think this could become a blockbuster across both ITP and combined indications. Contextually speaking, I think there's about 50,000 patients eligible for ITP. So we're really excited by this differentiated profile and bringing it to patients as quickly as possible.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Okay. We'll help you dream a little in a moment, Graham, but first, Houman, maybe respond to tolebrutinib.

speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: I'll start before Paul breaks out in song. I'm going to just take the question on tolebrutinib, and thanks for the question, Graham. It is truly multifaceted. So, first part of the question was on scenarios. We have two relapsing remitting trials running, GEMINI I and II. But let me just dimensionalize this across those indications. Firstly, in terms of relapse and remitting, you make an excellent point about previous failures. However, we must remind everyone that in terms of penetration across the CSF by a physical property, our biological properties exceed others in the space by a significant margin. Secondly, when we talk about mechanism, patients who come off standard of care and go on to tolebrutinib have shown continued reductions in neurofilament light. These parameters enable us to remain optimistic yet cautious about the role of tolebrutinib in both relapsing and progressive diseases. The short answer is we will see where we get with GEMINI I and II, but we should remember that the regulatory landscape is well understood in the context of relapsed independent progression rate. So the short answer is, we will see where we get with GEMINI I and II, but I would strongly suggest that the regulator and the patients truly care about disease progression. Regarding the progressive disease, we are cautiously optimistic due to the data we've discussed, and there is no AUBAGIO comparator arm in that population. This provides a unique opportunity for us.

speaker: Brian Foard
title: SVP, U.S. Commercial Operations
content: I think the question on price is really about value, more than anything else. It starts with the fact that there's no more differentiated program in MS than this tolebrutinib program. We will provide commentary on pricing at that particular time but not now.

content: No, Brian. What I can tell you is I don't want to quantify the EPS, but we are very confident about it. I think we have the building blocks, starting with the growth profile we have today. speaker: Paul Hudson

The dosing interval is particularly interesting. Importantly, off-drug disease suppression is significant. These three remarks represent our optimism: One, the differentiators we're observing regarding early atopic disease without progression; two, the biologic mechanisms impacting all ethnicities; three, driving this through multiple indications, some of which we'll read out this year. The quick answer to your question is that we are driving the studies diligently, featuring four Phase IIIs, which we aim to complete in an orderly manner. speaker: Paul Hudson

speaker: Operator

speaker: Brian Foard

content: Yeah. I think there's a couple of things in there. Firstly, as we mentioned before, bringing a new therapy like this to any patient population requires educating both the patients and the physicians. There’s a lot to be done, where it's not just about coming in and taking share. It will require some bio penetration. We've seen this very well in atopic dermatitis, where we are nearly eight years in, and the bio-penetration rate is 11%. So it takes time, and it takes effort. The good news regarding cost, there are efficiencies since we are already set up across the alliance, deeply ingrained in pulmonologist offices in all countries. OpEx will contribute efficiently, because this will be our second indication in the same offices. We will spend to support this launch, as it is absolutely critical for us to reach as many patients as possible, and we certainly see some efficiencies in our setup.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Thank you. ALTUVIIIO share any business coming from non-factor and any comments on Mimi?

speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: Yeah. A couple of things there. I think this always comes back to the patient and their unmet medical need. If you think about the patient population here, effectiveness is key. Previously, when speaking about HEMLIBRA, it played more of a convenience role than anything else. While effective, it was more about convenience being the first subcutaneous product. ALTUVIIIO is doing exceptionally well. We couldn't be more pleased with the launch progress because the physician and patient population are really responding to the profile that we're bringing, which is better efficacy with near-normal factor levels over an entire week through a single dose therapy. We're seeing switches from all patient types, regardless of their current therapies. Specifically, we're primarily transitioning from factors, where we believe all patients on factors should move to ALTUVIIIO. The factor marketplace represents about 60% to 65% of the market today, which is where we primarily capture business. Out of our switches, two-thirds are coming from competitors, and one-third from LOCTITE again, a factor that should switch. This relates to HEMLIBRA and, regarding the competitor coming in, I believe HEMLIBRA should be more concerned about that. However, we are taking about 10% of our business from HEMLIBRA, but this isn't what we anticipated necessarily. The feedback from physicians over 80% of whom prescribed have been positive, and we anticipate continuous growth moving forward. So again, we're off to a strong start as we approach almost the one-year mark with ALTUVIIIO.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Thank you, Brian. And as we observe market developments, you're right; I believe we took more patients from HEMLIBRA than expected, possibly because they are trying to match efficacy to the weekly standard, which brought a similar convenience. I believe that this month or possibly with eight-week intervals could create a new benchmark as well. The market is undoubtedly gravitating towards convenience versus efficacy in the trade, so I think we're well-situated. Next question.

speaker: Emmanuel Papadakis

content: Thank you for your questions. I'd like to start with cash flow. In the first quarter, we faced significant restructuring costs exceeding €700 million. How do you anticipate that will affect the full year, and what portion of that will be in cash? speaker: François-Xavier Roger
title: CFO
content: Let me start. Good afternoon, Emmanuel. On the cash flow, so the decrease in Q1 is mostly from a lower gross to net on Lantus. As you know, we are booking lower, but we have to pay cash flow for rebate on a higher base at least in Q1. We will also see some impacts in Q2 and Q3. This has significantly affected our cash flow in Q1, and there will be a bit of it in the next two quarters. Obviously, this will continue for the full year. This is a kind of one-off that will impact our cash flow throughout the full year. I don't want to quantify it because there are other moving parts, but this is a fairly significant one-off impact. On the restructuring costs, it's related to many of the projects we have already announced; part of it is obviously hitting France, as you know, which is in the public domain too. It's not necessarily a cash item at all that will be a significant issue in 2024. It's going to spread over the next two years, partly, but some of it could potentially hit towards the end of 2024 as well.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Thank you. Olivier, any comments on Tzield?

speaker: Olivier Charmeil
title: Head of General Medicines
content: Regarding Tzield, we see a positive evolution and slightly accelerating growth in terms of screening and infusion rates, Q1 versus Q4, where we have higher infusion rates in Q1. We have also seen more higher infusion in pediatric patients, which is a good signal for us, indicating progress. Infusions have accelerated, driven by enhanced field force execution and better coordination along the patient journey. Payers' coverage is solid and is not a barrier to utilization. We indicated from the start that this would be a slow burn. We’re shaping a market that previously didn’t exist due to a lack of treatment, which will take time. But we believe that it is worth the effort. It’s about creating awareness among patients and families, as well as with HCPs. We’re encouraged by the consensus guidelines being developed and the involvement of regulatory bodies that align medical societies towards guidelines. Overall, it will be a slow burn, but we are confident it will continue to progress. We believe it is worthwhile continuing to invest, reinforced by our communication with KOLs and clinicians who provide us confidence that Tzield, our first and only disease-modifying therapy in type 1 diabetes, is promising.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: I could add that we understood full well when we made the transaction. There is a reason why some small companies sell great medicines; it's because they cannot conduct this type of work over several years. The quarterly transitions are less a priority at the moment, but we are focused on screening numbers. We will see significant contributions from this medicine in the coming years, including up to 2026, 2027, 2028. Tzield will be a big deal for the company as we put in hard work. There's no current competition for a decade, and we don't need to rush this. We can work correctly which will set us up in the community for the CD40 ligand. We are excited with how guidelines and other developments are evolving. Next question.

speaker: Operator

speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: Thanks for the question, Seamus. Both points are deeply insightful. The first one is simple to answer: I can confirm that we are pleased with the liver tolerability profile of rilzabrutinib thus far and are confident taking it forward. Regarding MS, your observation is very astute; there may be interactions between the BTKI and the underlying biology in MS, which leads to differential signaling. I think that's a reasonable hypothesis, and we have data supporting it; it reflects clinical experience.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Thank you. On the business development and M&A point, we indicated the coverage of €2 billion to €5 billion range for bolt-ons, which is standard. We committed after Q3 last year that we would maintain R&D spending around €7.7 billion through 2024 and 2025. We don’t want to deviate from that plan; I think that would not be appropriate. We anticipate failures would open up capacity, resulting in potential bandwidth in 2025 and 2026. Most of the bigger studies will graduate as our pipeline expands, allowing us natural room to maneuver; therefore, you might see more energy in bolt-ons in early phases, given that this larger investment comes later, meaning we can absorb without losing commitments. Our balance sheet is good, and we need to leverage that, but we need discipline around our R&D budgets. I think it would be expected to keep guidance, and if opportunities arise, reallocating may be our priority. But demonstrating discipline post Q3 last year must remain our main concern going forward. We believe we can grow EPS and achieve other targets while also maintaining commitment as we prepare for the LOE of Dupixent when it arrives. Discipline will be our standard going forward in the coming years. Next question.

title: Operator

speaker: Jo Walton
title: Analyst
content: Excellent. Two quick questions then please. title: SVP, U.S. Commercial Operations
content: I think this question is great; it concerns the transition to many patients. The patient population is identified early in their lives, and they are already on therapies. So we expect to see this demographic switch from all types of therapy.

speaker: Thomas Triomphe
title: Head of North America
content: Regarding the next countries, what I can share is that we want to ensure we have enough supply for the three geographies of significant uptake last year, which are Spain, the U.S., and France. Moving forward, we already initiated the Southern Hemisphere season in Chile and some regions of Australia. For Northern Hemisphere 2024, I expect more European countries to follow suit. However, it's essential to understand that for each new immunization, there are specific national processes to establish recommendations via recommending bodies, which is why I cannot disclose specific country names yet. speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: Regarding Frexalimab, your query is well placed. We've positioned Frexalimab primarily for MS and type 1 diabetes, confirming its efficacy in these larger indications. We remain confident it can deliver clinical utility, but we have explored adjacent areas where we think there’s a biological rationale for potential impacts. I wouldn’t interpret the recent failure in Sjögren’s as a failure of the Frexalimab broader step. We are still solid in our larger indications.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Yes. We believe that developing pathways can lead to significant opportunities with our pipeline. Achieving success requires exploring many of these avenues where potential exists. We expect to see increasing interest in validating multiple pathways. This will help in the journey as we assess and refine as needed. Next question.

title: Analyst
content: Yes, thanks very much and for all the updates today. I have one question that I would appreciate some detail around. So the company has phase II readouts in IandI accelerating in 2025. Could you discuss key candidates that have the most commercial potential?

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO
content: Okay, David, thank you. I think Houman will start on the key readouts that you’re excited about, specifically focused on I&I in 2025, as you requested.

speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: It's tough to choose between our favorite candidates for 2025. Firstly, our notable advancement includes data for amlitelimab in various disorders, especially in alopecia. Another is our RIPK1 inhibitor for UC, presenting an intriguing biological opportunity. Lastly, I'm keen on our oral TNFR1 signaling inhibitor, which can address TNF treatment's classic needs with a lower side effect profile. Lunsekimig, our special asthma molecule, is also important. It combines modular targeting to enhance efficacy while ensuring durability, an element crucial in asthma therapy. I can't forget to mention our RSV products, as we are as excited about vaccines as we are about our pharma products. We find that our pipeline is increasingly pivotal as we look forward to busy years in R&D.

speaker: Paul Hudson
title: CEO

title: CFO

speaker: Paul Hudson

speaker: Peter Verdult
title: Analyst
content: Thank you. Peter Verdult from Citi. Two questions, Peter. So, with that in mind, I'd like to ask two follow-up questions for Houman on rilza and tolebrutinib. I understand you can't discuss too much ahead of data presentations, but could you share your assessment of how competitive you believe the rilza data in ITP will be against incumbent molecules like Promacta, especially considering Promacta faces generic risks? Additionally, on tolebrutinib, in light of the late summer phase III readouts, how do you view the relative opportunities across readouts in remitting and progressive MS? KOL feedback suggests waning effect for both EVO and tole over time concerning gadolinium lesion reduction, indicating caution regarding positive results in relapsing/remitting MS. Progressive MS presents the greatest unmet need, but randomized Phase II data remains absent. Is it mainly the brain penetration and NFL data that you find gives you confidence regarding the progressive trials, or would you like to share any additional points?

speaker: Houman Ashrafian
title: Head of R&D
content: Thanks for these insightful questions. First, I believe that the existing standard care options, including Promacta, are meaningful; they’ve played critical roles in ITP treatment. However, they don't get to the disorder's core, as you mentioned; mechanistically, rilzabrutinib targets B-cell suppression while concurrently addressing Fc-gamma receptor-mediated destruction of the platelets. Hence, just building up platelet counts without also addressing fatigue or the underlying issues is crucial. So this is the potential we see for rilza. It presents a significant advantage over current therapies. Regarding tolebrutinib, I admit I find it frustrating that the focus shifts as development progresses. As for progressive disease, we find that nearly nothing offers substantial value for secondary progressive MS. Today, patients are significantly undertreated or often misclassified to gain therapy. If tolebrutinib proves effective, its risk/reward is already evident. For relapsing disease, some discussions may materialize if we meet the eligibility in the GEMINI studies, which we are well poised to achieve with appropriate evaluation.

speaker: Brian Foard
title: SVP, U.S. Commercial Operations
content: The value question is about context—there's no more differentiated program in MS than this tolebrutinib initiative. We shall see how the graphs develop down the line while determining appropriate pricing when the time is right.
